body_ar:
لقد جاءت صفات الإثبات مفصلة في القرآن والسنة، أما النفي فلم يفصل إلا في نفي الصاحبة والشريك والوالد والولد، وقد كان منهج السلف في التعامل مع صفات الله تعالى إثباتها والوقوف عند النصوص الواردة بها من غير تشبيه ولا تعطيل.
نفي وجود الصاحبة والوالد والولد لله عز وجل.
المقصود من نفي وجود الكفء لله:
ثم قال: (ليس لَهُ كُفُواً أَحَدٌ) وهذا تقرير لكل ما سبق، ولا يحتاج إلى العطف فيه، يمكن أن تقول: لماذا لم يقل: (وليس لَهُ كُفُواً أَحَدٌ)؟ والجواب: أن معنى أنه (ليس لَهُ كُفُواً أحد): أنه لا صاحبة له ولا ولد ولا والد؛ لأن الكفء هو النظير، يقال: الكفو بالواو، والكفء بالهمزة، والكفؤ بضمتين، وهذه كلها مقروءة، فقراءة نافع و ابن كثير و ابن عامر (كفؤاً) بالهمزة، وقراءة الكوفيين: (كفواً) بالواو لكن شعبة يقرؤها (كفْواً) بإسكان الفاء بالإسكان وغيره يقرؤها بالضم. والمقصود بهذا أمران: أحدهما: نفي التشبيه مطلقاً؛ لأن الكفاءة مقتضية لقدر من الاشتراك في الشبه، فالبشر من جهة التمثيل أكفاء، لا أحد منهم يزيد على آخر بعضو مثلاً، بل هم صورة واحدة؛ ولهذا قال الشافعي رحمه الله: الناس من جهة التمثيل أكفاء أبوهم آدم والأم حواء والثاني: وهو المقصود الأساس من نفي الكفء: أنه لا يمكن أن يكافئه ولا أن يناظره أحد حتى يتزاوج معه...
body_en:
*[Site synopsis]* The attributes of affirmation have come set out in detail in the Qur'an and the sunnah. As for negation, it has not been set out in detail except in the denial of a consort, a partner, a progenitor and offspring. The way of the early generations in dealing with the attributes of God, exalted is He, was to affirm them and to stop at the texts in which they have come, without likening Him to creation and without stripping Him of them.

## The denial that God, mighty and majestic, has a consort, a progenitor or offspring

## What is meant by the denial that God has an equal

Then He said: {and there is none equal to Him}. This is a confirmation of everything that preceded, and it needs no connective in it. You might say: why did He not say "and there is none equal to Him"? The answer is that the meaning of "there is none equal to Him" is that He has no consort, no offspring and no progenitor — because "al-kufʾ" is the counterpart.

One says "al-kufw" with a wāw, "al-kufʾ" with a hamzah, and "al-kufuʾ" with two ḍammahs; and all of these are read. The reading of Nafiʿ, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Amir is "kufuʾan" with the hamzah, and the reading of the Kufans is "kufwan" with the wāw — except that Shuʿbah reads it "kufwan" with the fāʾ vowelless, with sukūn, while others read it with ḍammah.

Two things are meant by this. The first is the denial of any likeness whatsoever, because equality requires some measure of shared resemblance. Human beings, in respect of their being formed alike, are equals: not one of them exceeds another by a limb, for instance; rather they are one and the same form. It is for this that al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, said:

*People, in respect of their being formed alike, are equals; their father is Adam and the mother is Eve.*

The second — and this is the fundamental thing meant by the denial of an equal — is that no one can be His equal or His counterpart so as to marry with Him …

flags.context: the site's synopsis, on the way of the early generations
options: without likening Him to creation and without stripping Him of them
flags.note: A formula that names the two errors the position defines itself against, and it is the fault line between the theological schools. 'تشبيه' is asserting a likeness between God and creation; 'تعطيل' is emptying the divine attributes of content. 'Anthropomorphism' is too narrow for the first, since the likeness at issue need not be to a human being. The second has no English noun at all, so the English renders it as a clause. Style guide section 12: the record takes a side in a dispute between Muslim schools, and it does so in the site's voice rather than the Sheikh's.

flags.arabic: فقراءة نافع و ابن كثير و ابن عامر (كفؤاً) بالهمزة ... لكن شعبة يقرؤها (كفْواً) بإسكان الفاء بالإسكان
flags.context: the treatment of the canonical readings
options: render the readings exactly, transliterating each variant so the distinctions survive
summarise the variants in a single sentence
flags.note: A passage on the canonical readings of the Qur'an (qirāʾāt), which cannot be translated without transliterating the variants, since the whole content is the difference between kufwan, kufʾan and kufuʾan. Two things for a reviewer. The Arabic says 'بإسكان الفاء بالإسكان', repeating the same word in two forms, which is a transcription doubling of the class flagged at record 715; it is preserved in body_ar and rendered once in the English. And the letter named is 'الفاء', but the vowel at issue in these variants falls on the fāʾ of كُفُوًا, so the naming is correct as served and has not been altered.

flags.arabic: الكفاءة مقتضية لقدر من الاشتراك في الشبه ... حتى يتزاوج معه
flags.context: the argument drawn from the word kufʾ
options: equality requires some measure of shared resemblance … so as to marry with Him
compatibility entails a degree of likeness … such that marriage could occur
flags.note: 'كفاءة' carries a technical sense in family law — the doctrine of the suitability of spouses — and the argument here runs deliberately through it: the verse denies God an equal, equality implies a shared measure, and the specific equality the word names is the one that makes marriage possible, which is why the verse is read as denying Him a consort. An English rendering that loses the marriage sense loses the argument. 'Equality' has been used rather than 'compatibility' so that the same English word carries both the verse and the reasoning.

Either the first is a heading over the whole lesson and the second over its first section, or text has dropped out between them. Both have been rendered as headings and nothing has been supplied; a reviewer should note that the subject of the first heading — consort, progenitor, offspring — is treated only incidentally in what survives.

The attribution to al-Shafi'i is the lecturer's and is kept exactly as he gives it, with no source and no verification added. translator_notes: One of a run of fourteen records, IDs 734-747, the series 'The Names and Attributes', all built to the same template and all excerpts. Each carries a site-written synopsis, then a section heading, then the opening formula and the first lines of a lesson, and then breaks off on an ellipsis; the full text sits behind a .doc download in the /medias/doc/esmawesivat-* series, numbered 1 to 14 in the same order as the IDs. None of the SEF aliases in this run carries a timestamp, so no upload date can be read from them.

The source's final line, 'تحميل المادة' ('download the material'), is the label of a download link in the page furniture, not part of the text. It is recorded as source_download_link and omitted from body_ar and body_en.
Qur'anic renderings here are interpretive and are not a substitute for the Arabic.

The record has no opening formula: it begins in the middle of a commentary on Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ, with 'Then He said', which refers to the preceding verse of the sura and not to any person. The English keeps the bare 'Then He said' and supplies nothing.

The Qur'anic phrase is quoted three times in the passage with three different vocalisations, which is the point being made; the English quotes it once inside braces where the lecturer first cites it and thereafter in ordinary quotation marks, because the later occurrences are citations of a word and not of scripture.
Proper names are given without diacritics in body text per style guide section 2: Nafi, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Amir, Shu'bah, al-Shafi'i.
No ruling term from the five-rulings table appears anywhere in the record.
